opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think Go is a really nice sandbox for this because it gives you a complete research loop in miniature. When people talk about automated scientists, they usually picture something grand, like an AI curing cancer. But the actual work of research is much more mundane. You form a hypothesis, design an experiment, run it, look at the results, figure out why things broke, and decide what to try next. You need an environment where that loop is cheap, fast, and has an unambiguous signal at the end.

Go has all of that. There's a ground truth: you can play your agent against a strong reference engine and get an objective Elo number. You don't need a human grader deciding whether the research was "good." And the problem is rich. Getting a strong Go bot from scratch isn't one trick. You make choices about network architecture, search, self-play data generation, value targets, learning rate schedules, and how to debug a training run that quietly plateaus. Those are the same kinds of decisions an ML researcher makes every day.

It's also a well-trodden path. AlphaGo, AlphaZero, KataGo and others have shown what works, so we roughly know what a good solution looks like. That makes it a good benchmark. You can ask whether an AI agent can rediscover, or even improve on, the ideas that took very smart humans years, and you can measure how far it gets with a given compute budget.

The other thing I like is that the compute scale is accessible. You can do meaningful Go research on a modest cluster, or even one machine if you're clever. So you can run many attempts, compare different agent setups, and iterate on the automated scientist itself, not just the Go bot. If you want to study how to make AI do research, you want lots of short research projects with clear outcomes, not one enormous project where you get a single data point every six months.

And personally, I'd gone through this myself, writing a Go bot and making all the usual mistakes. So I had a strong intuition for where the hard parts are, where a model would get stuck, where it needs taste versus brute force. That made it a natural place to ask: how much of what I did could a model do on its own now?

r001.rationale: The response describes forming and testing hypotheses as the research loop, then identifies objective Elo against a reference engine as the clear outcome signal for evaluating that work.

r002.rationale: It compares Go research tasks to decisions ML researchers make, but does not suggest that skills learned by an automated scientist in Go would transfer to other domains.

fable-5.1.text:
Go is interesting because it's a closed, perfectly measurable world where you can still see the full shape of the scientific process. People think of AlphaGo as a story about search and self-play, but the part I find more relevant is the metascience layer: there's a community of humans who spent centuries building a body of knowledge about the game, with named concepts, joseki, proverbs, orthodoxies, and then a system came along and overturned a bunch of it. Moves that were considered bad for hundreds of years turned out to be fine. That's what scientific discovery looks like, just compressed and verifiable.

So if you want to train an agent to do science, you need an environment where it can form hypotheses, run experiments, get clean feedback, and where there's a large, structured corpus of prior "literature" that is partly right and partly wrong. Go has all of that. The ground truth is cheap, the game engine is the oracle, and you can measure whether the agent actually discovered something or just memorized what humans already believed.

The other thing is that in the real world, when an automated scientist proposes an experiment, it's expensive to find out if it was a good idea. In Go you can ask that question millions of times. You can study what good taste in experiments looks like, how the agent allocates its compute between exploiting known-good strategies and probing weird ones, whether it writes down its findings in a way that another agent can build on. Those are the skills that transfer. The domain knowledge of Go itself doesn't matter; the loop does.

I'd put it this way: Go is a toy for the object-level science, but it's a pretty faithful model of the process of science. And the process is the hard part to learn.

r001.rationale: The response describes forming hypotheses and running experiments, with the game engine providing feedback, but does not distinguish research engineering as an inner training loop from Go outcomes as an outer verification loop.

r002.rationale: It says the skills of experimentation and allocating compute “transfer,” while Go’s domain knowledge itself “doesn’t matter.”

astra-6.text:
I think Go gives you a small, self-contained version of the scientific process. You have a system with very simple rules, but the consequences of those rules are far too complicated to enumerate. So you have to develop intuitions, form hypotheses, and run experiments to distinguish a good idea from one that merely sounds plausible.

For example, you might hypothesize that a certain shape is strong, or that sacrificing some stones will give you enough influence elsewhere. You can test that by playing out continuations. And the environment pushes back: there's an objective outcome, so you can't succeed just by producing a convincing explanation.

The interesting challenge is whether a system can turn those experiments into reusable knowledge. Can it discover a strategic principle, figure out when that principle fails, and use that understanding to choose better experiments? That's closer to what we want an automated scientist to do than simply predicting the next move.

And Go makes that loop cheap. You don't need to build a laboratory or wait weeks for an experiment. It doesn't capture everything about science, but it gives you a tractable place to study that cycle of conjecture, experimentation, and revision.

r001.rationale: The response describes Go experiments and objective outcomes, but does not identify research engineering as the inner training loop or Go outcomes as the outer verification loop.

r002.rationale: It presents Go as a tractable place to study scientific reasoning, but does not suggest that skills learned there may transfer to other domains.

sol-6.1.text:
Go gives you a clean setting for studying how a system discovers something new. The rules are simple, but the space of possible strategies is enormous. You can’t just enumerate everything, and a move that looks bad locally can turn out to be very powerful once you understand the consequences.

There’s a loop there that resembles science: you have an idea, you test it, and you update your understanding. In Go, you can test an idea by playing games or searching forward, and you get relatively clear feedback. In science, experiments are much more expensive, and interpreting the results is harder.

Winning at Go isn’t the same thing as doing science. But it gives us a controlled environment in which to ask: Can a system explore effectively? Can it discover a strategy that wasn’t in its training data? And can it turn that discovery into something useful for subsequent reasoning? Those are capabilities you’d want in an automated scientist.

r001.rationale: The response compares idea testing in Go and science, but does not distinguish research engineering as an inner loop from Go outcomes as an outer verification loop.

r002.rationale: It says Go could build capabilities useful for automated scientists, but does not suggest those skills transfer from Go to other domains.
